questions.q: What does `sudo apt update` actually do?
options: Removes packages that are no longer needed
Upgrades every installed package to its latest version
Refreshes the local list of available packages and versions from configured repositories, without installing or upgrading anything
questions.explain: apt update only refreshes package metadata from repositories. It does not install or upgrade packages — that's apt install or apt upgrade.

questions.q: What is the difference between `apt remove nginx` and `apt purge nginx`?
options: remove uninstalls the package but leaves its configuration files; purge also removes those configuration files
remove deletes config files; purge keeps them
purge only works on dnf, not apt
There is no difference between the two
questions.explain: apt remove uninstalls the package binaries but leaves configuration files in place in case you reinstall later. apt purge removes those configuration files as well.

questions.q: Why doesn't `dnf install nginx` usually need a separate metadata-refresh step beforehand, unlike `apt`?
options: dnf automatically refreshes its cache when it detects the metadata is stale
dnf cannot refresh metadata at all
questions.explain: dnf checks whether its cached repository metadata is stale and refreshes it automatically as needed, unlike apt where update is typically run as an explicit separate step.

questions.q: Which command confirms the exact installed version of nginx and which repo it came from, on an Ubuntu system?
questions.explain: apt list --installed shows currently installed packages with their version; filtering with grep nginx isolates the entry for that package.

questions.q: What is the dnf equivalent of `apt upgrade` (upgrading every installed package to its latest version)?
questions.explain: dnf update upgrades all installed packages to their latest available versions, functionally equivalent to apt upgrade on Debian/Ubuntu systems.
